claims.text: Integrating high-throughput ab initio simulations with machine-learning optimization can be used to design refractory high-entropy alloys.
The hybrid approach can identify refractory HEA compositions that are intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight.
The hybrid approach efficiently maps complex composition–structure–property relationships.
First-principles simulations can capture atomic-level bonding in candidate refractory HEAs.
First-principles simulations can capture phase behavior in candidate refractory HEAs.
Machine-learning algorithms can optimize refractory HEA composition for targeted mechanical properties.
Interatomic bonding characteristics and phase stability are directly related to nanostructural and microstructural features that determine strength and ductility.
High-throughput simulations generate detailed atomic-scale data on candidate alloy phases and bonding energies.
Simulated phase and bonding-energy data can be used to train a machine-learning model.
The trained model can predict trends in mechanical strength across a vast refractory HEA composition space.
The trained model can predict trends in ductility across a vast refractory HEA composition space.
The trained model can predict density trends across a vast refractory HEA composition space.
Predicted property trends can guide the selection of optimal refractory HEA compositions.
Alloys selected by the hybrid approach will have greater tensile strength than alloys designed using traditional thermo-kinetic methods.
Alloys selected by the hybrid approach will have greater ductility than alloys designed using traditional thermo-kinetic methods.
Alloys selected by the hybrid approach will have lower density than alloys designed using traditional thermo-kinetic methods.
The method's effectiveness depends on the availability of sufficient computational data for the alloy system.
Performance under extreme environmental conditions may not be established by simulations conducted only under the stated initial conditions.
